<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sheng Ran
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Physics, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO 63130, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Reconstructing Future Research Initiative
</span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">August 24, 2026</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their apparent diversity, modern machine learning methods can be reduced to a remarkably simple core
principle: learning is achieved by continuously optimizing parameters to minimize or maximize a scalar objective
function. This paradigm has been extraordinarily successful for well-defined tasks where goals are fixed and evaluation criteria are explicit. However, if artificial systems are to move toward true autonomy—operating over long horizons and across evolving contexts—objectives may become ill-defined, shifting, or entirely absent. In such settings, a fundamental question emerges: in the absence of an explicit objective function, how can a system determine whether its ongoing internal dynamics are productive or pathological? And how should it regulate structural change without external supervision?
In this work, we propose a dynamical framework for learning without an explicit objective. Instead of minimizing external error signals, the system evaluates the intrinsic health of its own internal dynamics and regulates structural plasticity accordingly. We introduce a two-timescale architecture that separates fast state evolution from slow structural adaptation, coupled through an internally generated stress variable that accumulates evidence of persistent dynamical dysfunction. Structural modification is then triggered not continuously, but as a state-dependent event. Through a minimal toy model, we demonstrate that this stress-regulated mechanism produces temporally segmented, self-organized learning episodes without reliance on externally defined goals. Our results suggest a possible route toward autonomous learning systems capable of self-assessment and internally regulated structural reorganization.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the remarkable achievements of modern artificial intelligence, a fundamental limitation remains: today’s AI systems are not truly autonomous. Across supervised <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, reinforcement <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, and self-supervised paradigms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, learning ultimately relies on the continuous optimization of an explicit loss or objective function defined—directly or indirectly—by human designers. While this paradigm has proven extraordinarily successful for well-specified tasks, it presupposes the existence of clearly defined goals and stable optimization landscapes. However, genuine open-ended learning often unfolds without predefined objectives. In biological evolution, human cognition, and creative discovery, goals frequently emerge only retrospectively. Agents do not begin with a fixed scalar objective; instead, they navigate uncertain, evolving, and partially defined environments where both tasks and representations may change over time.</p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p">Over the past decades, several approaches have attempted to move beyond externally specified task losses. Broadly, these efforts can be grouped into three categories. The first category replaces explicit task objectives with intrinsic scalar quantities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>. Examples include mutual information maximization, prediction error minimization, entropy maximization, contrastive divergence, and variational free energy minimization. Although these methods do not depend on externally labeled targets, learning remains driven by the optimization of a scalar function defined over system states or representations. In this sense, the objective is reformulated rather than eliminated. The second category adopts local or biologically inspired update rules such as Hebbian learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, self-organizing maps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. These rules often appear objective-free at the algorithmic level. However, in many cases, their dynamics can be shown to correspond to the descent of an implicit energy or Lyapunov function under certain assumptions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. Even when no explicit loss is written, learning frequently remains governed by an underlying scalar potential structure. The third category, including the free energy principle and active inference frameworks, explicitly formalizes adaptation as the minimization of variational free energy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>. Although philosophically ambitious, these approaches likewise retain optimization as the central organizing principle.</p>
</div>
<div id="p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p3.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, current mainstream approaches to learning without external objectives typically replace task-specific losses with alternative scalar potentials. Learning remains largely characterized as optimization within a fixed state space under the influence of a scalar-driven dynamical field. For many engineering purposes—training models, solving well-defined tasks, or optimizing performance metrics—this paradigm is both effective and appropriate. However, if the goal is to construct truly open-ended, self-evolving cognitive systems, deeper questions arise.</p>
</div>
<div id="p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p4.1" class="ltx_p">Optimization-based learning implicitly assumes that:</p>
<ul id="S0.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S0.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S0.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S0.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">a meaningful scalar objective exists,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S0.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S0.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S0.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">the representational space is sufficiently stable,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S0.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S0.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S0.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">and improvement corresponds to descending (or ascending) a fixed potential landscape.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="p4.2" class="ltx_p">Yet autonomous intelligence in biological systems exhibits additional properties: it maintains itself, reorganizes its internal structure, revises its representational assumptions, and escapes unproductive modes of reasoning—even in the absence of clearly defined objectives. Such systems do not merely optimize within a static landscape; they may alter the landscape itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p5.1" class="ltx_p">This leads to a fundamental question: when no explicit loss function is available, how can a system determine whether its ongoing reasoning process is productive or pathological?
Current AI systems rarely confront this question because they are designed as tools rather than autonomous agents. Human operators define objectives, schedule training, reset models, switch datasets, and intervene when systems fail. Under this regime, AI does not need to evaluate the quality of its own reasoning dynamics—this responsibility is outsourced to humans. However, this assumption breaks down in settings characterized by long-horizon autonomy (e.g., autonomous scientific discovery or exploratory agents), continual task evolution, or open-ended creative exploration. In such environments, the central problem shifts from performance optimization to structural self-assessment: determining whether the system’s internal organization remains conducive to sustained reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p6.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we study how a learning system can evaluate and regulate its own reasoning dynamics without being continuously driven by a single scalar gradient objective. Rather than framing learning solely as parameter adjustment within a fixed landscape, we treat it as the regulation of dynamical regimes. We propose a learning framework that incorporates phase-gated, discrete, and structurally constrained plasticity. Instead of continuously optimizing a global scalar objective, the system monitors dynamical signatures of its own reasoning process and selectively triggers structural reorganization when pathological regimes are detected. We show that such a framework enables a system to regulate and reorganize potentially unproductive reasoning trajectories, even in the absence of an externally specified objective.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18581v1/Figure1.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/228;" width="476" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Two-Timescale Dynamical Framework.</span> Fast dynamics <math id="S0.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x(t)</annotation></semantics></math> evolve within a structural landscape defined by slow parameters <math id="S0.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. The system continuously performs intrinsic evaluation of its own dynamical health (e.g., freezing, non-ergodicity, irreversibility), generating an accumulated stress signal <math id="S0.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math>.When stress exceeds a critical threshold <math id="S0.F1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, structural update is triggered, leading to a reconfiguration of the landscape <math id="S0.F1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\rightarrow\theta^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\rightarrow\theta^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>. The updated structure reshapes the effective landscape in which subsequent fast dynamics unfold.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span>A Two-Timescale Dynamical Framework</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The key question we address here is: instead of minimizing an externally defined error, can a system regulate its plasticity based on the intrinsic health of its own dynamics?
To investigate this possibility, we develop a minimal two-timescale dynamical framework in which fast state evolution and slow structural adaptation are explicitly separated.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the presence of an explicit objective function, failure modes collapse into a single signal provided by the loss. In the absence of an explicit objective, however, this collapse no longer holds. A system may fail either because it has not explored sufficiently within a viable structure, or because the structure itself is incapable of supporting effective reasoning. In the latter case, thinking may continue indefinitely without producing meaningful progress. Crucially, these two failure modes are indistinguishable at the level of outcomes alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Distinguishing between them therefore requires evaluating the thinking process itself, rather than its results. Without external feedback or task-specific loss, the only available signal is the intrinsic behavior of the system’s own internal dynamics. For this reason, “thinking” must be modeled not as a static input–output mapping, but as a physical process unfolding in time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To formalize this idea, we introduce a coupled dynamical framework with a fundamental separation of timescales as shown in Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. This separation reflects a core cognitive distinction: transient thought activity evolves rapidly within a given representational structure, while the structure itself changes slowly and only under specific conditions. Such a distinction allows the system to assess whether failures arise from the dynamics of thinking within a structure, or from the structure itself.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.1 </span>System Equations and Multiscale Dynamics</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define the cognitive architecture through two coupled dynamical components representing fast and slow variables of the system.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fast State (Thinking Variable).</span>
The variable <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the instantaneous state of ongoing thought, such as neural population activity or working memory configurations. Its dynamics describe how the system explores, evaluates, and transitions between mental states within a fixed representational structure. We model this process as an overdamped Langevin dynamics,</p>
<table id="S1.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dot{\mathbf{x}}=-\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}V(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})+\bm{\eta}(t)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></msub><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>𝜼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dot{\mathbf{x}}=-\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}V(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})+\bm{\eta}(t),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> defines an effective cognitive landscape shaped by the structural parameters <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\eta}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\eta}(t)</annotation></semantics></math> represents intrinsic fluctuations or environmental noise.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Slow Structure (Structural Parameters).</span>
The variable <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> encodes the persistent structural organization that shapes the landscape of thought, such as representational geometry or synaptic connectivity. Its evolution is modulated by a plasticity control signal <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)</annotation></semantics></math>, which regulates when and how structural modification occurs:</p>
<table id="S1.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dot{\bm{\theta}}=m(t)\cdot\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x},\bm{\theta})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dot{\bm{\theta}}=m(t)\cdot\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x},\bm{\theta}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The specific form of <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)</annotation></semantics></math>—whether continuously active, state-dependent, or event-driven—will be treated as a design choice to be analyzed later.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This formulation establishes a bidirectional feedback loop. The structural parameters <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> determine the geometry of the cognitive landscape and thus constrain the trajectories of thought <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}(t)</annotation></semantics></math> (downward causality). Conversely, the long-term statistical properties of these trajectories—rather than immediate outcomes—regulate whether the structure itself should be revised (upward causality). This separation enables the system to tolerate transient thinking failures while responding decisively to persistent structural inadequacy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.2 </span>The Cognitive Stress Field</h3>

<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To prevent the system from overreacting to transient fluctuations or short-lived failures, structural modification should depend on temporally integrated information about the quality of thinking. To achieve this, we introduce an intrinsic Cognitive Stress Field, <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math>, which mediates between fast dynamics and structural change.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The stress field <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is a latent dynamical variable that accumulates tension when the quality of the thinking process degrades over time. Unlike traditional loss functions in machine learning—which rely on task-specific labels or external objectives—the evolution of <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math> depends on intrinsic dynamical health, with an additional internal cost term that discourages excessive plasticity:</p>
<table id="S1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dot{Z}=\Phi(\mathcal{Q}(\cdot))+\underbrace{\Psi(m,\Delta\theta)}_{\text{plasticity cost}}-\gamma Z," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>plasticity cost</mtext></munder></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dot{Z}=\Phi(\mathcal{Q}(\cdot))+\underbrace{\Psi(m,\Delta\theta)}_{\text{plasticity cost}}-\gamma Z,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a set of dynamical descriptors evaluated over a finite time window, such as freezing, non-ergodicity, or irreversibility. <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi(m,\Delta\bm{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi(m,\Delta\bm{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> represents an intrinsic cost of plasticity, and <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> represents a dissipation rate that prevents unbounded stress accumulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Structural plasticity is then regulated through the interaction between the stress field and the control signal <math id="S1.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. In a simple threshold-based implementation, one may define,</p>
<table id="S1.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)=\Theta\!\big(Z(t)-Z_{c}\big)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.621em;" width="0.621em"><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)=\Theta\!\big(Z(t)-Z_{c}\big),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S1.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the Heaviside step function and <math id="S1.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a critical stress level.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, this threshold rule should be understood as one possible realization rather than a mandatory choice. More generally, <math id="S1.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)</annotation></semantics></math> may represent a continuous modulation function, a probabilistic trigger, or an event-based mechanism derived from the stress dynamics. The key principle is that structural adaptation is governed by internally accumulated evidence of persistent dynamical pathology, rather than by instantaneous errors or externally defined objectives.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">With this construction, structural change becomes state-dependent: transient or recoverable thinking failures may dissipate without modifying the structure, while sustained degradation in dynamical health gradually accumulates stress and increases the likelihood of structural reorganization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span>Criteria for “Good Thinking”: Dynamical Descriptors</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having established a dynamical framework for thinking, we now face a central question: how can a system evaluate the quality of its own thinking in the absence of external objectives or task-specific feedback? In our framework, “good thinking” is not defined by performance, but by the intrinsic properties of the thinking dynamics themselves. We propose that “good thinking” is defined by the structural properties of the state-space trajectory <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. To quantify the intrinsic health of these dynamics, we introduce three physically motivated metrics, which together govern the evolution of the cognitive stress field <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math>, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ II Criteria for “Good Thinking”: Dynamical Descriptors ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a></p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18581v1/badness.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/105;" width="476" height="105" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intrinsic dynamical failure modes.</span> (Left) Freezing. The system becomes confined to a narrow region of the landscape. (Middle) Non-ergodicity. The trajectory explores only a subset of the accessible landscape, failing to visit other basins over long timescales. (Right) Irreversibility. The trajectory undergoes a directed drift or structural bias such that previously accessible regions cannot be revisited.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">II.1 </span>Freezing Index (<math id="S2.SS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>): Quantifying Attractor Collapse</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Persistent “looping” or “stagnation” in a narrow region of the state space is a hallmark of suboptimal cognition. To quantify this “early-freezing” phenomenon, we define the <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Freezing Index</span> based on the local covariance of the fast state:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="F_{T}=\exp\left(-\lambda\cdot\text{Tr}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}[t-W:t]})\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{T}=\exp\left(-\lambda\cdot\text{Tr}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{x}[t-W:t]})\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\Sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚺</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\Sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> is the covariance matrix of the trajectory calculated over a sliding window <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is a scaling sensitivity parameter.</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As the trajectory collapses into a point-like attractor or a low-dimensional limit cycle, <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Tr}(\mathbf{\Sigma})\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Tr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝚺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Tr}(\mathbf{\Sigma})\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{T}\to 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{T}\to 1</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating “frozen thinking.”</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A healthy thinking process maintains a sufficiently high trace, representing active exploration within the current landscape.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">II.2 </span>Non-Ergodicity (<math id="S2.SS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>): Measuring Exploratory Scope</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> detects local collapse, a system may still be trapped within a suboptimal basin of attraction, failing to explore the broader relevant state space. We quantify this using the <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Non-Ergodicity</span> index, defined as the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the empirical occupancy distribution and a reference distribution:</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E_{T}=D_{KL}\left(p_{T}(\mathbf{x})\parallel q(\mathbf{x})\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{T}=D_{KL}\left(p_{T}(\mathbf{x})\parallel q(\mathbf{x})\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{T}(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{T}(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> is the empirical distribution of states visited during the interval <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> represents a target or uniform distribution over the reachable state space. A high <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> value signifies that the thinking process is non-ergodic, remaining localized in a subset of the configuration space and ignoring potentially superior solutions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">II.3 </span>Irreversibility (<math id="S2.SS3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>): Assessing Cognitive Flexibility</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Drawing from stochastic thermodynamics, we interpret the “flexibility” of thought through the lens of time-reversal symmetry. “Bad thinking” is often characterized by a “mental slide”—a strongly irreversible process where the system is driven into a state from which it cannot easily backtrack. We define the <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Irreversibility Index</span> as:</p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{T}=\ln\frac{\mathcal{P}(\text{forward path})}{\mathcal{P}(\text{backward path})}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>forward path</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>backward path</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{T}=\ln\frac{\mathcal{P}(\text{forward path})}{\mathcal{P}(\text{backward path})}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the path probability of the trajectory. In a computational context, this can be approximated by the discriminability between forward and time-reversed sequences of <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
<ul id="S2.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{T}\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{T}\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math> indicates near-reversible, “liquid” dynamics, suggesting a high capacity for error correction and logical(backtracking).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">High <math id="S2.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to high entropy production, signaling a brittle, “one-way” cognitive process that is prone to becoming trapped in “mental dead-ends”.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span>Continuous versus Stress-Gated Plasticity</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having established an intrinsic, dynamical criterion for evaluating the quality of thinking—independent of any external task or loss—the next question concerns how a system should adapt when its internal dynamics degrade.
Within our framework, structural adaptation is regulated by the control signal <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. In principle, <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)</annotation></semantics></math> may take different forms: it may be continuously active, weakly modulated, probabilistic, or discretely triggered.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the presence of an explicit loss function, continuous parameter optimization is natural: every update step is locally validated by the objective. Persistent adjustment is justified because the loss provides a reliable gradient signal that distinguishes improvement from deterioration at each moment. Indeed, in most contemporary learning paradigms, the implicit assumption is continuous plasticity. Formally, this corresponds to fixing</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(t)\equiv 1," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(t)\equiv 1,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">so that structural parameters evolve at every time step in response to moment-to-moment dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the absence of an explicit objective, however, this justification disappears. Structural plasticity is no longer anchored to an externally defined direction of progress. The system must rely solely on internal dynamical signals, which are inherently noisy and fluctuating. Under such conditions, continuously active plasticity implicitly assumes that moment-to-moment deviations always warrant structural modification. This assumption is nontrivial.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Without an objective function to separate transient fluctuations from genuine structural inadequacy, always-on adaptation risks conflating two qualitatively different situations:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Local instability within an otherwise adequate structure.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Persistent structural mismatch that cannot be resolved by internal exploration alone.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">If plasticity is continuously active, these two cases are treated identically. Structural parameters are adjusted at every moment, even when short-term fluctuations may self-correct. In effect, structure is never allowed to remain stable long enough to be properly tested. The system cannot distinguish between “explore more within the current structure” and “change the structure itself.”</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This observation suggests a more general principle: in the absence of an external objective, plasticity should not be permanently active. Instead, structural modification should require accumulated internal evidence that the current organization is persistently inadequate. Such evidence must integrate over time to avoid reacting to transient noise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">A gated or state-dependent plasticity mechanism naturally implements this requirement. By allowing structural updates only when an internally accumulated signal exceeds a threshold, the system creates a temporal separation between two phases:</p>
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Exploration within a fixed structure.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Structural reorganization in response to sustained internal stress.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">This separation is not introduced as a biological analogy, but as a logical consequence of operating without an explicit objective. When improvement cannot be externally validated at every step, structure must be granted periods of stability; otherwise, adaptation becomes indistinguishable from noise-driven drift.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span>Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now construct a minimal toy model based on the principles developed above, which we term the Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics (SGCD) model. SGCD is designed to illustrate how high-dimensional internal states can spontaneously give rise to repeatable, low-dimensional behavioral patterns when the system is endowed with (i) a global stress-like variable and (ii) a gated plasticity mechanism that intermittently reshapes internal structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The model is not trained on external data and does not optimize an explicit objective function. Instead, it self-organizes by alternating between two modes: (a) fast intrinsic dynamics that explore the current structural landscape, and (b) discrete plasticity episodes that are triggered endogenously when accumulated stress signals persistent dynamical failure. Technically, SGCD is a discrete-time instantiation of the generic continuous-time framework introduced earlier, with the Langevin drift implemented via a contractive recurrent update and the stress field realized as an exponential moving average.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Before presenting the specific equations of the SGCD model, it is important to clarify how the general criteria for “good thinking” introduced in the theoretical section are instantiated in this minimal setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The freezing, non-ergodicity, and irreversibility indices defined in Sec. II are intended as principle-level diagnostics. They formalize, at a conceptual level, what it would mean for an autonomous system to evaluate the intrinsic health of its own thinking dynamics without reference to external tasks or losses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In the present toy model, we do not attempt to implement all three criteria in their full generality. Instead, we adopt a reduced and computationally tractable realization that captures the most salient failure modes relevant for spontaneous structural reorganization. Specifically, freezing is detected through relative stagnation in a noise-corrected velocity measure, while non-ergodicity is approximated by the absence of a stable prototype structure in the recent trajectory. The irreversibility criterion, while conceptually important, is not explicitly evaluated in this minimal model and is left for future extensions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This reduction preserves the core logic of the framework while keeping the model analytically transparent. Stress is generated by persistent dynamical pathologies, rather than instantaneous fluctuations, and structural plasticity is gated only when fast exploration repeatedly fails to organize into coherent internal patterns.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.1 </span>Microscopic state and fast dynamics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The microscopic state is an <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vector <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, representing the system’s moment-to-moment cognitive state. It evolves under a recurrent interaction matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}</annotation></semantics></math> with additive noise:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x(t+1)=(1-\alpha)x(t)+\alpha\tanh\big(W(t)x(t)\big)+\sigma\eta(t)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>tanh</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x(t+1)=(1-\alpha)x(t)+\alpha\tanh\big(W(t)x(t)\big)+\sigma\eta(t),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> controls update speed and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> sets the noise level.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is symmetric with zero diagonal, and its scale is stabilized by enforcing a target spectral radius (details below). This prevents the fast dynamics from collapsing (vanishing interactions) or diverging (runaway amplification).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.2 </span>Behavioral observables: motion and prototype strength</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At each time step, the model evaluates two windowed observables from the recent trajectory <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="X_{t-\tau:t}={x(t-\tau),\dots,x(t-1)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{t-\tau:t}={x(t-\tau),\dots,x(t-1)}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Noise-corrected velocity. A velocity proxy measures how rapidly the state moves in configuration space:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prototype strength. A simple order parameter quantifies whether the trajectory has a consistent mean direction:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
