<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Large <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> indicates the system is hovering around a biased prototype (more structured); small <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> indicates a more balanced or dispersed trajectory.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.3 </span>Badness and Stress accumulator <math id="S4.SS3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The model defines a scalar badness core <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{\rm core}(t)\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>core</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\rm core}(t)\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> that reflects two conditions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Plateau / stagnation</span>: the system is moving unusually slowly compared to a lagged baseline of <math id="S4.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\rm eff}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>eff</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\rm eff}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Low prototype</span>: the system lacks strong prototype structure relative to a slow baseline of <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Concretely, a plateau score rises when <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\rm smooth}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>smooth</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\rm smooth}(t)</annotation></semantics></math> falls below a fraction of a lagged baseline <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\rm base}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>base</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\rm base}(t)</annotation></semantics></math>, and a low-prototype factor rises when <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(t)</annotation></semantics></math> sits below an adaptive good level derived from a slow baseline <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\rm base}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>base</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\rm base}(t)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The product forms the core badness:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{\rm core}(t)\sim\text{Plateau}(t)\times\text{LowProto}(t)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>core</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>Plateau</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mtext>LowProto</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\rm core}(t)\sim\text{Plateau}(t)\times\text{LowProto}(t),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">with optional flooring.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This construction makes badness a functional diagnostic: the system is not merely noisy or slow; it is slow and not forming a stable prototype.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">A global stress variable <math id="S4.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math> integrates total badness (including plasticity costs) on a slow timescale:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t+1)=(1-\lambda_{Z})Z(t)+\lambda_{Z}B_{\rm total}(t)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>total</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t+1)=(1-\lambda_{Z})Z(t)+\lambda_{Z}B_{\rm total}(t).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.2" class="ltx_p">Stress therefore encodes recent history and can remain elevated even if instantaneous badness fluctuates.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.4 </span>Gated plasticity</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Plasticity is not always on. Instead, the model opens a plasticity episode when stress exceeds a threshold:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Normal gating: when the system is armed and <math id="S4.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z&gt;Z_{\rm on}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>on</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z&gt;Z_{\rm on}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Override trigger: if stress remains high and fails to improve over a long window, the system can open a gate even without being armed, preventing prolonged stagnation under elevated stress.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The system becomes re-armed only after stress falls below <math id="S4.I3.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{\rm off}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>off</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{\rm off}</annotation></semantics></math> (hysteresis).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A gate triggers a commit window of length <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\rm commit}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>commit</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\rm commit}</annotation></semantics></math>, during which plasticity is ON at every step. After a gate, a refractory window prevents immediate retriggering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This creates discrete cognitive events: short plastic episodes separated by longer periods of stable fast dynamics.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18581v1/SGCD.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/333;" width="476" height="333" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stress-gated cognitive dynamics.</span> (a) Badness and stress accumulator <math id="S4.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the global time. (b) Plastic rent and plastic update cost as a function of the global time. (c) A zoomed view of the gating signal. The red dots represent the gate trigger. (d) The norm of the connectivity matrix <math id="S4.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|W|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|W|</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the global time. (e) Gate-aligned heatmaps of badness. The horizontal axis denotes time relative to the gate, and the vertical axis indexes individual episodes. (f) Gate-aligned heatmaps of stress.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.5 </span>Structural proposal and plasticity update</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When a gate opens, the model proposes a structural target <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\rm target}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>target</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\rm target}</annotation></semantics></math> from the recent trajectory window. It uses the demeaned covariance:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=\frac{1}{\tau}X_{c}^{\top}X_{c},\quad X_{c}=X-\langle X\rangle," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>τ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\frac{1}{\tau}X_{c}^{\top}X_{c},\quad X_{c}=X-\langle X\rangle,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">then symmetrizes, removes the diagonal, optionally soft-thresholds small entries, and critically rescales the matrix to a fixed spectral radius <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{\rm target}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>target</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{\rm target}</annotation></semantics></math>. This normalization is the key stability fix: it prevents the learning target from collapsing toward zero magnitude.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">During plasticity, the system performs a small convex step toward the target:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\leftarrow(1-\epsilon)W+\epsilon W_{\rm target}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>target</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\leftarrow(1-\epsilon)W+\epsilon W_{\rm target},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.2" class="ltx_p">followed by symmetry/zero-diagonal enforcement and spectral-radius normalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">During a plasticity episode, <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\rm target}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>target</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\rm target}</annotation></semantics></math> may be refreshed every <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\rm refresh}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>refresh</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\rm refresh}</annotation></semantics></math> steps using the most recent trajectory window <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="X_{t-\tau:t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{t-\tau:t}</annotation></semantics></math>, allowing the structural update to reflect changes in the fast dynamics over the course of the episode.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.6 </span>Plasticity has a price</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Plasticity is not free. The model includes two explicit costs:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rent cost <math id="S4.I4.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\rm on}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>on</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\rm on}</annotation></semantics></math>: a constant penalty paid whenever plasticity is ON.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Update cost <math id="S4.I4.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{W}</annotation></semantics></math>: proportional to the relative RMS change of <math id="S4.I4.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> per step:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{cost}_{\rm update}\propto c_{W}\frac{{\rm RMS}(W_{\rm new}-W_{\rm old})}{{\rm RMS}(W_{\rm old})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>cost</mtext><mi>update</mi></msub><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>RMS</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>RMS</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>old</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{cost}_{\rm update}\propto c_{W}\frac{{\rm RMS}(W_{\rm new}-W_{\rm old})}{{\rm RMS}(W_{\rm old})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Total badness is:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{\rm total}(t)=\text{clip}\Big(B_{\rm core}(t)+\text{rent}(t)+\text{updateCost}(t),0,1\Big)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>total</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>clip</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>core</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>rent</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>updateCost</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\rm total}(t)=\text{clip}\Big(B_{\rm core}(t)+\text{rent}(t)+\text{updateCost}(t),0,1\Big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Because stress integrates <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{\rm total}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>total</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\rm total}</annotation></semantics></math>, this creates a tradeoff: plasticity can reduce future badness, but it temporarily increases badness via costs—so the system cannot benefit from plasticity unless structural changes compensate for this price.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.7 </span>Two safety mechanisms: early-abort and forced rearm</h3>

<div id="S4.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To avoid two failure modes (wasting plasticity, or becoming permanently static after one ineffective gate), the model adds:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I5" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I5.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early-abort (within a gate). Inside a plasticity episode, after a short delay <math id="S4.I5.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\rm abort}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>abort</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\rm abort}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model measures the stress drop since gate onset, <math id="S4.I5.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta Z=Z(t_{gate})-Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta Z=Z(t_{gate})-Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S4.I5.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta Z</annotation></semantics></math> is below a threshold while stress remains above <math id="S4.I5.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{on}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{on}</annotation></semantics></math> (and, optionally, if badness has not improved), the plasticity window is terminated early. This prevents long, unproductive plasticity runs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I5.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I5.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I5.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Forced rearm probes. If a gate is aborted for insufficient improvement, the model schedules a forced rearm: after cooldown it tries a shorter “probe” gate of length <math id="S4.I5.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\rm probe}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>probe</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\rm probe}</annotation></semantics></math>, up to a maximum number of attempts per episode. This prevents the system from entering a state where it never gates again simply because the earlier gate did not succeed.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18581v1/continous.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/286;" width="476" height="286" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Continuous Plasticity Dynamics.</span> (a) Badness and stress accumulator <math id="S4.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the global time. (b) Gate, plastic rent and plastic update cost as a function of the global time. (c) The norm of the connectivity matrix <math id="S4.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|W|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|W|</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the global time. (d) Gate-aligned heatmaps of badness. The horizontal axis denotes time relative to the gate, and the vertical axis indexes individual episodes. (e) Gate-aligned heatmaps of stress.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">IV.8 </span>Results and Discussion</h3>

<div id="S4.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our results are summarized in Fig. 1. The global time series of total badness <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and stress <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(t)</annotation></semantics></math> exhibit repeated cycles of stress accumulation followed by relaxation (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ IV.4 Gated plasticity ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>a and Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ IV.4 Gated plasticity ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>b). Crucially, these relaxation phases are temporally aligned with discrete gate events that activate structural plasticity. Between gates, the system evolves solely under fast intrinsic dynamics and noise, during which stress gradually builds up. This behavior demonstrates that adaptation in the SGCD model is not continuous, but event-driven: structural updates are sparse and are triggered only when accumulated stress exceeds a critical threshold.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A closer view of the gating signal (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ IV.4 Gated plasticity ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>c) shows that each gate initiates a finite commit window during which plasticity is active. The duration of these windows is bounded and independent of the instantaneous stress level once the gate is triggered. This design enforces a clear separation of time scales: fast dynamics explore the state space under a fixed structure, while slow structural plasticity operates episodically. Early-abort and refractory mechanisms further prevent runaway or redundant updates, ensuring that plasticity remains selective and economical.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To determine whether gate events merely coincide with random fluctuations or correspond to reproducible dynamical transitions, we align trajectories around gate onset and visualize them as heatmaps (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ IV.4 Gated plasticity ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>e and Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ IV.4 Gated plasticity ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>f). If gates were triggered by incidental fluctuations, alignment would not reveal any systematic structure: individual episodes would remain heterogeneous and no consistent pre–post pattern would emerge. Instead, we observe a stereotyped temporal profile across events. Both badness and stress reliably peaks near gate onset and subsequently decays over hundreds of steps. Although individual episodes are not identical, they share a common dynamical motif. This alignment therefore reveals something nontrivial: gate onset defines an internally generated event time that organizes the dynamics into repeatable episodes. The system does not simply fluctuate continuously under noise; it alternates between accumulation phases and relaxation phases with a consistent temporal structure. In this sense, gates do not merely label high-stress moments—they segment the ongoing dynamics into coherent transitions between metastable regimes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the norm of the connectivity matrix <math id="S4.SS8.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|W|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|W|</annotation></semantics></math> remains bounded over long times (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ IV.4 Gated plasticity ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>d), but more importantly, it exhibits a piecewise-stable pattern: extended plateaus of nearly constant magnitude interrupted by discrete structural shifts. During plateau phases, plasticity is inactive and the structural landscape remains effectively frozen, allowing the fast dynamics to unfold within a stable representational substrate. Structural changes occur only during brief gated episodes, after which the system settles into a new metastable configuration. This punctuated pattern of structural evolution is nontrivial. Although plasticity is repeatedly invoked, the system does not drift continuously. Instead, it alternates between consolidation phases and reorganization phases, producing a temporally segmented structural trajectory rather than a diffusive one. The resulting connectivity dynamics therefore reflect episodic restructuring rather than gradual erosion or unstructured fluctuation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To isolate the role of stress-gated plasticity, we perform a control experiment in which plasticity is continuously active at all times, while all other components of the model are kept identical.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Under continuous plasticity, the system remains dynamically stable: stress and badness do not diverge, and the connectivity norm stays bounded over long times (Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ IV.7 Two safety mechanisms: early-abort and forced rearm ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). Transient fluctuations and recurring peaks are clearly present in the global time series, indicating that continuous plasticity is sufficient to support ongoing adaptation and short-lived pattern formation. In this sense, the system remains responsive and dynamically active.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p7.1" class="ltx_p">However, the qualitative organization of these dynamics differs fundamentally from the gated case. Although stress and badness exhibit repeated peaks that may visually resemble gated episodes, these fluctuations arise from ongoing noise-driven perturbations coupled to continuous weight updates. They do not correspond to discrete structural transitions. The system remains in a state of persistent drift rather than alternating between consolidation and reorganization phases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p8.1" class="ltx_p">This difference becomes clearer when examining the structural trajectory. Unlike the gated system, the connectivity norm <math id="S4.SS8.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|W|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|W|</annotation></semantics></math> does not exhibit extended plateaus separated by abrupt shifts. Instead, it fluctuates continuously without identifiable metastable regimes (Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ IV.7 Two safety mechanisms: early-abort and forced rearm ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>c). The absence of structural plateaus indicates that no stable internal configuration is ever temporarily consolidated; plasticity is constantly modifying the substrate on which fast dynamics unfold.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p9.1" class="ltx_p">To further probe whether reproducible learning episodes emerge, we apply the same gate-centered alignment analysis used in the gated system (Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ IV.7 Two safety mechanisms: early-abort and forced rearm ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>d and Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ IV.7 Two safety mechanisms: early-abort and forced rearm ‣ IV Stress-Gated Cognitive Dynamics ‣ Learning Beyond Optimization: Stress-Gated Dynamical Regime Regulation in Autonomous Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>e). Because plasticity is always active, each time step can be treated as a putative “episode onset,” and we align trajectories accordingly. In contrast to the gated case, no reproducible event-centered temporal structure emerges. The aligned heatmaps exhibit diagonal stripe patterns, reflecting the underlying global oscillatory fluctuations of the system. However, these patterns are not anchored to the alignment point. Instead, they represent phase-drifting dynamics that persist independently of the chosen reference time. When averaged across aligned segments, no consistent pre–post transition centered at the putative onset appears. This result indicates that, although continuous plasticity sustains ongoing fluctuations and transient structure formation, it does not organize the dynamics into phase-locked learning events. The system remains temporally stationary and homogeneous rather than episodically segmented. Learning unfolds as a continuous drift rather than as internally demarcated transitions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, these results demonstrate that the SGCD model does more than evolve a collection of vectors under noise. The system self-organizes into a regime of punctuated adaptation, in which internally generated stress gates discrete episodes of structural plasticity. These gates segment the dynamics into reproducible learning events, rather than allowing adaptation to proceed diffusely in time. Importantly, this organization emerges without any externally imposed task, reward signal, or objective function. The system does not converge to a predefined attractor or optimize a fixed loss; instead, it develops a temporal structure of exploration, stress accumulation, and structural reconfiguration. In this sense, what is “learned” is not a static weight configuration, but a repeatable dynamical motif that governs when and how structural change occurs. SGCD therefore provides a minimal yet concrete example of how meaningful temporal organization—and episodic learning—can arise from unguided dynamics through stress-regulated plasticity alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span>Conclusion and Outlook</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we have proposed a minimal dynamical framework for learning in the absence of an explicit objective function. Rather than treating learning as continuous optimization of a predefined loss, we model it as a two-timescale process in which fast state evolution unfolds within a structural landscape, while slow structural change is regulated by intrinsic evaluation of the system’s own dynamical health. Plasticity is not assumed to be perpetually active, but becomes a state-dependent phase triggered by accumulated internal stress.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This shift reframes the problem of learning. Instead of asking how to minimize error, we ask how a system can remain dynamically viable when no external criterion is available. The central claim is that meaningful structural organization can emerge not from task-specific supervision, but from the regulation of internal failure modes such as freezing, non-ergodicity, and irreversibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although the present model is intentionally minimal, it suggests several broader implications. First, the framework provides a principled route toward genuinely autonomous systems. As artificial agents move beyond closed tasks and externally curated training regimes, the assumption of a fixed objective function becomes increasingly untenable. Long-horizon exploration, scientific discovery, creative reasoning, and continual adaptation all involve phases in which goals are unknown or only retrospectively defined. In such regimes, the capacity to evaluate and regulate one’s own dynamical organization may become more fundamental than objective optimization itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Second, the separation between fast and slow dynamics offers a structural perspective on stability and plasticity. Rather than tuning a continuous learning rate, the system organizes learning into phases of exploration and phases of reconfiguration. This temporal segmentation may provide a foundation for developing architectures that preserve internal coherence over long durations while remaining capable of decisive structural change.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Third, the stress-regulated mechanism opens the door to new mathematical questions. What classes of intrinsic dynamical metrics are sufficient to detect structural inadequacy? Under what conditions does gated plasticity produce stable nontrivial structure rather than drift or collapse? How do different stress accumulation rules affect long-term organization? These questions point toward a broader theory of self-regulated dynamical systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Several extensions naturally follow. The current framework can be generalized to high-dimensional neural networks, to stochastic control settings, or to agents embedded in partially observable environments. It may also be connected to biological theories of neuromodulation, sleep-dependent consolidation, and developmental critical periods, where structural change is episodic rather than continuous.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">More fundamentally, this work suggests a conceptual distinction between optimization-driven learning and viability-driven learning. The former assumes a predefined target; the latter assumes only the necessity of maintaining coherent internal dynamics. Whether such viability-based regulation can support open-ended intelligence remains an open question. The present framework provides a minimal testbed for exploring that possibility.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
